title: Hey Mom…
subtitle: Recipes and stories from 28 years of feeding the people I love.
author: Missy
intro:
My name is Missy Delaria, and I learned to cook on the banks of the Niagara River. I grew up in Grand Island, a suburb just outside Buffalo, New York, in a house that looked across the water to Canada. We were a typical family of four — my mother stayed home, my father worked, and my sister was six and a half years older than me, off doing her own things. Truthfully, my mom and grandmother were not big cooks. I treasure the couple of their recipes I still make today, but the kitchen was mostly mine to figure out. I really learned to cook from three places: from Suzie — Mrs. Wiles, a housekeeper in our neighborhood — who gave me my foundation and the real how-to of it; a little bit from my mom; and a great deal from myself, by experimenting, trying things, and simply having the drive and the desire to make good food for the people I love. I started cooking avidly in my early twenties — I can still picture myself baking in my little apartment, turning out sugar cookies and fudge brownies to give away as gifts, made with love and joy, and finding my footing with a few good pasta and pork dishes. It all began with love and curiosity, and it has never stopped. I've never boxed my cooking into one tradition. There's American in it, European, a little Southern — but honestly, nothing is strictly defined. My cooking is defined by taste, and by how much my family and friends enjoy it. That, to me, has always been the only measure that matters.

Years later, I met my husband in 1989, when we were college sweethearts. We married in 1995 in Wayzata, Minnesota, bought a wonderful little house in Deep Haven, and began building a life of our own. In August of 1997 we welcomed our first child, Kendall, and in September of 1999 we completed our family with our twins, Stockton and Larkin — and just like that, we were a family of five. When the children arrived, we had a decision to make: would I keep working, or stay home? We chose for me to stay home, and I have been devoted to that choice ever since.

Cooking in our family always started with one simple desire: to have us all together at the table every single night. Even when the children were babies, we ate dinner together. My rule was that I did not cook multiple meals — the family food was the family food, and the kids ate everything. Nothing was made special just for them. They certainly had their favorites, and once they were old enough they served themselves and could take a 'no thank you helping,' because the way I cooked was balanced and nutritious and I wanted them to have every part of what their growing bodies needed. Each child would fix their plate, carry it to their place, and wait until their father and I had ours, so that we were all seated at the same time. No one rushed through dinner. And every night, we went around the table and each shared one good thing and one bad thing from our day. That little ritual taught us something I hold dear: that good things are meant to be celebrated by the people you love, and the hard things can be solved — or simply comforted — by the people you love. We kept that table, and that tradition, all the way through high school, even when the kids were busy with lives of their own.

Feeding a family of five on a single income took real preparation and thought. It took creativity and a budget that worked. Every week I would sit down and plan our meals, then plan the grocery shopping around them, always making sure there were healthy things in the refrigerator for lunches and snacks. We were lucky enough to have little refrigerators that belonged to the kids, stocked with things like string cheese, juice boxes, Go-Gurts, fruit cups, and applesauce. They were allowed to help themselves to one without asking — and after that, they had to come find me. I took being their mom, and their father's wife, very seriously, and all of it — the planning, the prep, the energy — went into the meals my kids still come back to me for.

Feeding real people also means cooking around real tastes, and ours kept me on my toes. Honestly, my husband is the pickiest eater of us all — no condiments, no cream sauces, no cheese — which is a challenge, because those are exactly the things kids love to pile on their food. But I always found a way, and everyone always had something at the table they were happy to eat. Later in life, our youngest became gluten-free for medical reasons, and I set out to remake our favorites without gluten and to teach myself how to bake gluten-free — especially for her, the one who always swore she had a 'dessert pocket' that simply hadn't been filled yet. You'll find that many of the recipes in this book carry those lessons with them.

For twenty-eight years, my work has been raising our children and feeding our family — putting nutritious, wonderful-tasting, fun food on the table every single day. Food became the center of our home: the everyday dinners, the lunches and after-school snacks, the holidays, the parties, and all the friends and family who gathered around our table along the way. This book is everything I learned in those years, from the technique Suzie first taught me to the dishes my own kids grew up on. And that is exactly where this book gets its name. To this day, my grown children will text me out of the blue: 'Hey Mom…' — and then those three little dots — 'can you send me the recipe for…' It's always one of the things they grew up eating. This book is my answer to every one of those messages, gathered at last in one place. More than anything, it's an invitation. I want to welcome you into my years of experience at the stove — and I hope, in some small way, it helps with yours.

section_blurbs.Let's Make It Easy: Shortcuts, swaps, and smart little tricks for putting genuinely good food on the table without the fuss.
